solution:
[Textbook misprint: the book concludes that "the radius of the spherical ball is increasing at the rate of \(\frac{1}{36}\) cc/sec". The unit is wrong: \(\frac{dR}{dt}\) is a length rate and should read cm/sec; cc/sec is the unit of the GIVEN \(\frac{dV}{dt}\), evidently carried over. The value \(\frac{1}{36}\) is correct and the downstream working is unaffected.]

Let \(R\) be the radius, \(S\) be the surface area and \(V\) be the volume of the spherical ball.
\(V = \frac{4}{3}\pi R^{3}\) . . . (I)
Differentiate w. r. t. \(t\)
\(\frac{dV}{dt} = \frac{4\pi}{3} \cdot \frac{d}{dt}(R^{3})\)
\(4\pi = \frac{4\pi}{3} \cdot 3R^{2} \frac{dR}{dt}\) . . . [Given \(\frac{dV}{dt} = 4\pi\) cc/sec ]
\(\frac{dR}{dt} = \frac{1}{R^{2}}\) . . . (II)
When volume is \(288\pi\) cc.
i.e. \(\frac{4}{3}\pi \cdot R^{3} = 288\pi\) we get, \(R^{3} = 216 \Rightarrow R = 6\) . . . [From (I)]
From (II) we get, \(\frac{dR}{dt} = \frac{1}{36}\)
So, the radius of the spherical ball is increasing at the rate of \(\frac{1}{36}\) cm/sec.
Now, \(S = 4\pi R^{2}\)
Differentiate w. r. t. t.
\(\frac{dS}{dt} = 4\pi \frac{d}{dt}(R^{2}) = 8\pi R \frac{dR}{dt}\)
So, when \(R = 6\) cm
\(\left[\frac{dS}{dt}\right]_{R = 6} = 8\pi(6) \frac{1}{36} = \frac{4\pi}{3}\)
\(\therefore\) Surface area is increasing at the rate of \(\frac{4\pi}{3}\) cm\(^{2}\)/ sec.
note: A radius changes in cm/sec; the line still printed cc/sec, which its own note calls wrong.

solution: The line \(x+y=0\) has slope \(-1\) (inclination \(135^\circ\)). A required line through the origin makes angle \(\alpha\) with it, so its slope is \(m=\tan(135^\circ\pm\alpha)\). Then \(m\) satisfies (with \(m=y/x\)) a quadratic whose sum and product give the pair. Sum of slopes \(=\tan(135^\circ+\alpha)+\tan(135^\circ-\alpha)\) and product \(=\tan(135^\circ+\alpha)\tan(135^\circ-\alpha)\). Using \(\tan(135^\circ+\alpha)=\dfrac{-1+\tan\alpha}{1+\tan\alpha}\) and \(\tan(135^\circ-\alpha)=\dfrac{-1-\tan\alpha}{1-\tan\alpha}\): the product is \(\dfrac{(-1+\tan\alpha)(-1-\tan\alpha)}{(1+\tan\alpha)(1-\tan\alpha)}=\dfrac{1-\tan^2\alpha}{1-\tan^2\alpha}=1\), and the sum is \(\dfrac{-(1-\tan\alpha)^2-(1+\tan\alpha)^2}{1-\tan^2\alpha}=\dfrac{-2(1+\tan^2\alpha)}{1-\tan^2\alpha}=-2\sec2\alpha\). Thus the pair is \(y^2-(\text{sum})xy+(\text{product})x^2=0\Rightarrow y^2+2\sec2\alpha\,xy+x^2=0\), i.e. \(x^2+2(\sec2\alpha)xy+y^2=0\). Hence proved.
note: The degree signs on 135 were missing (the next line has them).
